Neuroendocrine carcinoid tumors (often originating in the ileum with liver metastases) hypersecrete serotonin, producing carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, right-sided valvular heart disease) and massive urinary excretion of 5-HIAA.

• Option A is incorrect: Dopamine is metabolized to homovanillic acid (HVA).
• Option B is incorrect: Norepinephrine is metabolized to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and metanephrines.
• Option D is incorrect: Histamine is metabolized to N-methylhistamine and methylimidazoleacetic acid.
• Option E is incorrect: Acetylcholine is broken down to choline and acetate by AChE.

stem: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is treated with haloperidol, a high-potency dopamine D2 receptor antagonist. Three weeks later, he develops bilateral resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and masked facies. Concurrently, he reports bilateral breast enlargement and milky nipple discharge (galactorrhea). Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors in which two respective central dopaminergic pathways accounts for his parkinsonian symptoms and galactorrhea?

options.text: Mesolimbic pathway and Mesocortical pathway
Nigrostriatal pathway (parkinsonism) and Tuberoinfundibular pathway (galactorrhea)
Tuberoinfundibular pathway and Locus coeruleus projection
Raphe nuclei tract and Medial forebrain bundle
Area postrema and Tectospinal tract

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Nigrostriatal pathway (parkinsonism) and Tuberoinfundibular pathway (galactorrhea).

The brain contains four major dopamine pathways: (1) Nigrostriatal pathway (substantia nigra pars compacta to dorsal striatum): controls voluntary motor coordination; D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and drug-induced parkinsonism. (2) Tuberoinfundibular pathway (arcuate nucleus of hypothalamus to anterior pituitary): dopamine acts as prolactin-inhibiting factor; D2 blockade removes inhibition, causing hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and gynecomastia. (3) Mesolimbic pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens): mediates motivation/reward; overactivity causes positive symptoms of schizophrenia; D2 blockade reduces delusions/hallucinations. (4) Mesocortical pathway (VTA to prefrontal cortex): mediates cognition/affect; underactivity causes negative and cognitive symptoms.

• Option A is incorrect: Mesolimbic mediates psychosis/reward; mesocortical mediates negative symptoms.
• Options C, D, and E do not match the anatomy of parkinsonism and prolactin regulation.

stem: A 32-year-old woman experiences abrupt episodes of intense fear, heart palpitations, trembling, sweating, and feelings of impending doom. Functional neuroimaging during an episode reveals marked hyperactivation of a small, bluish-pigmented bilateral nucleus situated in the rostral dorsolateral pontine tegmentum beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. Which nucleus is this, and what is its primary neurotransmitter?

options.text: Substantia nigra; Dopamine
Locus coeruleus; Norepinephrine
Dorsal raphe nucleus; Serotonin
Basal nucleus of Meynert; Acetylcholine
Red nucleus; Glutamate

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Locus coeruleus; Norepinephrine.

The locus coeruleus ('blue place', due to neuromelanin granules) is located in the posterior rostral pons near the lateral floor of the 4th ventricle. It is the primary site of norepinephrine (NE) synthesis and source of noradrenergic projections throughout the neuraxis. Hyperactivity of the locus coeruleus is implicated in the pathogenesis of panic disorder, generalized anxiety, PTSD, and the physiological manifestations of opiate withdrawal. Conversely, its hypoactivity is associated with depression.

• Option A is incorrect: Substantia nigra is in the midbrain and synthesizes dopamine (degenerated in Parkinson disease).
• Option C is incorrect: Dorsal raphe nuclei are in the brainstem midline and synthesize serotonin.
• Option D is incorrect: Nucleus basalis of Meynert is in the basal forebrain and synthesizes acetylcholine (degenerated in Alzheimer disease).
• Option E is incorrect: Red nucleus is in the rostral midbrain tegmentum and controls upper limb flexor tone (rubrospinal tract).

stem: A 29-year-old man with severe major depressive disorder is started on sertraline. Therapeutic efficacy depends on increasing synaptic concentrations of serotonin throughout the central nervous system. Where are the neuronal cell bodies responsible for synthesizing the majority of central serotonin located?

options.text: Raphe nuclei of the brainstem midline
Caudate nucleus and putamen
Ventral tegmental area of Tsai
Lateral hypothalamic area
Dentate gyrus of the hippocampus

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Raphe nuclei of the brainstem midline.

The raphe nuclei form a contiguous column of serotonergic cell bodies lining the midline of the brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla). Rostral raphe nuclei (dorsal and median raphe in the midbrain/pons) project widely to the cerebral cortex, limbic system, and basal ganglia, regulating mood, sleep-wake cycles, appetite, and cognition. Caudal raphe nuclei (in the medulla) project down the spinal cord to modulate nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn (descending pain inhibitory pathway).

• Option B is incorrect: Striatum receives dopaminergic inputs and consists primarily of GABAergic medium spiny neurons.
• Option C is incorrect: VTA synthesizes dopamine.
• Option D is incorrect: Lateral hypothalamus synthesizes orexin/hypocretin (deficient in narcolepsy).
• Option E is incorrect: Hippocampal dentate gyrus is a primary site of adult neurogenesis and memory formation.

stem: An autopsy performed on a 38-year-old patient who died of untreated advanced HIV infection reveals microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells throughout the subcortical white matter (HIV-associated dementia). From which embryonic tissue origin are microglia derived, and what is their primary physiological function?

options.text: Neuroectoderm of the neural tube; structural support of the blood-brain barrier
Mesoderm (embryonic yolk sac myeloid progenitors); resident immune surveillance and phagocytosis
Neural crest; myelination of peripheral sensory axons
Endoderm; secretion of cerebrospinal fluid in the lateral ventricles
Surface ectoderm; maintenance of the ependymal ciliary carpet

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Mesoderm (embryonic yolk sac myeloid progenitors); resident immune surveillance and phagocytosis.

Unlike all other central nervous system cells (neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma), which originate from neuroectoderm, microglia are derived from mesodermal primitive myeloid progenitor cells in the embryonic yolk sac that migrate into the developing brain. Microglia function as the resident mononuclear phagocytes of the CNS, participating in immune defense, synaptic pruning during development, and clearing cellular debris following injury. In HIV encephalitis, HIV infects microglia/macrophages via CD4 and CCR5/CXCR4 coreceptors, causing them to fuse into characteristic multinucleated giant cells.

• Option A is incorrect: Astrocytes are neuroectodermal and support the BBB.
• Option C is incorrect: Schwann cells are neural crest-derived.
• Option D is incorrect: Choroid plexus epithelium produces CSF and is neuroectodermal.
• Option E is incorrect: Ependyma is neuroectodermal.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressive balance difficulties and intention tremor. Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of Friedreich ataxia, an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. In contrast to multiple sclerosis, in which demyelination is mediated by autoimmune destruction of oligodendrocytes, peripheral demyelinating polyneuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth) involve pathology of Schwann cells. What is a key structural difference between oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells?

options.text: A single Schwann cell can myelinate up to 50 individual CNS axons simultaneously, whereas an oligodendrocyte myelinates only a single axon internode
A single oligodendrocyte can myelinate internodes on up to 30 to 50 different CNS axons, whereas a Schwann cell myelinates only a single internode of a single PNS axon
Oligodendrocytes are derived from neural crest, while Schwann cells are derived from neuroectoderm
Schwann cells lack basement membranes, whereas oligodendrocytes possess thick collagenous basement membranes
Oligodendrocytes express myelin protein zero (P0), while Schwann cells exclusively express proteolipid protein (PLP)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. A single oligodendrocyte can myelinate internodes on up to 30 to 50 different CNS axons, whereas a Schwann cell myelinates only a single internode of a single PNS axon.

Oligodendrocytes (derived from neural tube neuroectoderm) are the myelin-producing cells of the CNS; each oligodendrocyte extends multiple cytoplasmic processes that wrap around and myelinate internodes on up to 30–50 separate axons. In contrast, Schwann cells (derived from neural crest) are the myelinating cells of the PNS; each myelinating Schwann cell envelops only ONE single internodal segment on ONE individual axon. Schwann cells also surround unmyelinated axons (Remak bundles) and promote peripheral axonal regeneration by forming Bands of Büngner.

• Option A is incorrect: It reverses the actual anatomy.
• Option C is incorrect: Oligodendrocytes derive from neuroectoderm, Schwann cells from neural crest.
• Option D is incorrect: Schwann cells are enveloped by an endoneurial basement membrane; oligodendrocytes lack a basement membrane.
• Option E is incorrect: Myelin protein zero (P0) is specific to PNS Schwann cell myelin; proteolipid protein (PLP) and myelin basic protein (MBP) dominate CNS myelin.

stem: During a neuroanatomy tutorial on brain barriers, the professor emphasizes that while the capillary endothelium of the brain parenchyma constitutes the blood-brain barrier (BBB), an entirely different layer forms the physiological barrier within the choroid plexus (the blood-CSF barrier). Which cellular component forms the true selective barrier in the choroid plexus?

options.text: Choroid plexus capillary endothelial cells joined by zonulae occludentes
Choroid epithelial cells (modified ependymal cells) joined by apical tight junctions (zonulae occludentes)
Pia mater connective tissue trabeculae
Pericytes covering choroid capillary venules
Arachnoid barrier cells lining the dural border

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Choroid epithelial cells (modified ependymal cells) joined by apical tight junctions (zonulae occludentes).

In the choroid plexus, the capillary endothelial cells are FENESTRATED, allowing free leakage of water, electrolytes, and plasma proteins into the stroma of the choroid plexus. However, the modified ependymal cells that cover the choroid villi (choroid epithelial cells) are bound tightly to one another by apical tight junctions (zonulae occludentes). This continuous epithelial monolayer forms the Blood-CSF Barrier, selectively controlling which ions and solutes are actively transported into the ventricular lumen to generate cerebrospinal fluid.

• Option A is incorrect: Capillaries of the choroid plexus are fenestrated and lack tight junctions (unlike parenchymal BBB capillaries).
• Option C is incorrect: Pial trabeculae are loose connective tissue elements.
• Option D is incorrect: Pericytes do not form the tight physiological barrier in the choroid plexus.
• Option E is incorrect: Arachnoid barrier cells seal the subarachnoid space from the dura, not the ventricular CSF.

stem: A 50-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy with cisplatin experiences intense nausea and vomiting within 30 minutes of infusion. Cisplatin triggers emesis by crossing into a circumventricular organ situated in the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle that lacks a blood-brain barrier. Which circumventricular organ functions as this chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting?

options.text: Area postrema
Organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT)
Subfornical organ
Pineal gland
Median eminence

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Area postrema.

Circumventricular organs (CVOs) are specialized brain structures situated around the 3rd and 4th ventricles that have fenestrated capillaries and lack a normal blood-brain barrier, allowing them to sample blood-borne chemicals. The Area Postrema is located on the dorsal surface of the caudal medulla in the floor of the 4th ventricle. It contains the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ), which detects circulating emetogenic toxins (such as chemotherapy drugs) and initiates the vomiting reflex via projections to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS).

• Option B is incorrect: OVLT senses plasma osmolarity and fever-inducing pyrogens (IL-1, PGE2).
• Option C is incorrect: Subfornical organ responds to circulating angiotensin II to regulate thirst and fluid balance.
• Option D is incorrect: The pineal gland secretes melatonin to regulate circadian rhythms.
• Option E is incorrect: The median eminence releases hypothalamic hypophysiotropic hormones into the hypophyseal portal circulation.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a large right frontal meningioma is brought to the emergency department after developing acute left leg and foot weakness, accompanied by sensory loss in the left foot and urinary urgency. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates subfalcine herniation with a 12 mm midline shift. Compression of which of the following cerebral arteries is responsible for her selective lower extremity deficits?

options.text: Middle cerebral artery (MCA), superior division
Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
Posterior cerebral artery (PCA), calcarine branch
Anterior choroidal artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation occurs when a unilateral mass lesion in the cerebral hemisphere forces the cingulate gyrus medially beneath the rigid, sickle-shaped free margin of the falx cerebri. This compresses the ipsilateral (and sometimes contralateral) anterior cerebral artery (ACA) against the falx. Because the ACA supplies the medial surface of the primary motor and somatosensory cortex (which represents the contralateral leg and foot on the cortical homunculus, as well as the micturition center in the medial frontal lobe), ACA compression results in contralateral leg weakness, sensory loss, and urinary incontinence.

• Option A is incorrect: MCA supplies the lateral cortical convexity (face and arm areas).
• Option C is incorrect: PCA is compressed in uncal (transtentorial) herniation, causing contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
• Option D is incorrect: Anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior limb of internal capsule and optic tract.
• Option E is incorrect: PICA supplies the lateral medulla and inferior cerebellum.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with progressive macrocephaly, clumsiness, and morning vomiting. Brain MRI demonstrates complete absence of the cerebellar vermis, cystic ballooning of the fourth ventricle occupying an enlarged posterior cranial fossa, and high tentorial insertion, associated with marked lateral and third ventricular dilation. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Chiari I malformation
Chiari II malformation
Dandy-Walker malformation
Holoprosencephaly
Arachnoid cyst of the middle cranial fossa

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Dandy-Walker malformation.

Dandy-Walker malformation is a congenital posterior fossa anomaly characterized by a classic triad: (1) Agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, (2) Cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle that fills the posterior fossa, and (3) An enlarged posterior cranial fossa with upward displacement of the tentorium and transverse sinuses. Obstruction of the foramina of Luschka and Magendie leads to non-communicating hydrocephalus in ~80% of patients, presenting with macrocephaly, delayed motor milestones, and signs of increased ICP.

• Option A is incorrect: Chiari I features cerebellar tonsillar ectopia >5 mm into the cervical canal without posterior fossa enlargement.
• Option B is incorrect: Chiari II features herniation of tonsils and vermis with a SMALL posterior fossa and myelomeningocele.
• Option C is incorrect: Holoprosencephaly is failure of forebrain separation.
• Option E is incorrect: Arachnoid cysts do not feature vermian agenesis or 4th ventricular cystic ballooning.

stem: An infant is born at 36 weeks gestation with severe craniofacial malformations, including hypotelorism, a single median maxillary central incisor, cleft lip and palate, and microcephaly. High-resolution cranial ultrasound reveals a monoventricular brain cavity with fusion of the frontal lobes and absence of the corpus callosum and septum pellucidum. Prenatal genetic testing confirms a heterozygous mutation in the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene. What developmental diagnosis best fits these findings?

options.text: Lissencephaly
Holoprosencephaly
Schizencephaly
Polymicrogyria
Dandy-Walker malformation

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Holoprosencephaly.

Holoprosencephaly (HPE) is a failure of the embryonic prosencephalon (forebrain) to cleave into two distinct cerebral hemispheres during the 5th to 6th weeks of gestation. It is classically associated with mutations in Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), and maternal diabetes/fetal alcohol syndrome. The condition exists on a spectrum: alobar (most severe; single monoventricular brain, fused thalami, cyclopia/proboscis), semilobar, and lobar. Facial anomalies ('the face predicts the brain') include cyclopia, ethmocephaly, cebocephaly, premaxillary agenesis, or a single central incisor.

• Option A is incorrect: Lissencephaly is smooth brain caused by abnormal neuronal migration.
• Option C is incorrect: Schizencephaly features full-thickness clefts in the cerebral hemispheres lined with gray matter.
• Option D is incorrect: Polymicrogyria features an excessive number of small, abnormally folded gyri.
• Option E is incorrect: Dandy-Walker malformation is a posterior fossa disorder (vermian agenesis).

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida delivers a stillborn male infant at 28 weeks gestation. Physical examination shows complete absence of the cranial vault (calvarium), with rudimentary brain tissue exposed to the amniotic environment and prominent, bulging orbits ('frog-like appearance'). Prenatal ultrasound had demonstrated profound polyhydramnios. What was the embryonic origin of this defect, and why did polyhydramnios develop?

options.text: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close; fetal polyuria due to impaired renal concentrating ability
Failure of the rostral (anterior) neuropore to close; absent fetal swallowing reflex due to destruction of brainstem swallowing centers
Failure of neural crest migration; lack of esophageal innervation preventing peristalsis
Premature fusion of the metopic suture; obstruction of the amniotic sac
Duplication of the notochord; mechanical compression of the umbilical cord

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Failure of the rostral (anterior) neuropore to close; absent fetal swallowing reflex due to destruction of brainstem swallowing centers.

Anencephaly is the most common lethal congenital CNS malformation, resulting from failure of the rostral (anterior) neuropore to close around embryonic day 25. The unclosed neural tube remains exposed to amniotic fluid, undergoing secondary hemorrhagic necrosis and degeneration (leaving only a vascular mass called area cerebrovasculosa), while the overlying calvarium and scalp fail to form. Polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) occurs because destruction of the forebrain and brainstem centers eliminates the fetal swallowing reflex, preventing the fetus from ingesting and recirculating amniotic fluid.

• Option A is incorrect: Caudal neuropore failure causes spina bifida; amniotic fluid is removed by fetal swallowing, not kidneys.
• Option C is incorrect: Neural crest failure causes Hirschsprung disease (distal bowel), not anencephaly.
• Option D is incorrect: Metopic craniosynostosis causes trigonocephaly, not anencephaly.
• Option E is incorrect: Notochord duplication causes split cord malformation.

stem: A 34-year-old dentist prepares to extract an infected lower molar surrounded by purulent exudate (pH 5.8). He infiltrates the adjacent tissue with 2% lidocaine (pKa = 7.9). Despite administering three separate cartridges, the patient continues to experience sharp, excruciating pain. What pharmacological principle explains why local anesthetics have markedly reduced clinical efficacy in infected, acidic tissue?

options.text: Bacterial enzymes rapidly metabolize lidocaine via extracellular amidases
The low extracellular pH shifts the equilibrium toward the charged (ionized) protonated form, severely reducing the uncharged fraction capable of crossing the lipid neuronal membrane
Acidic pH permanently denatures the voltage-gated sodium channel protein
Lidocaine precipitates into insoluble crystals at pH below 7.0
Local inflammation closes all nodes of Ranvier

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The low extracellular pH shifts the equilibrium toward the charged (ionized) protonated form, severely reducing the uncharged fraction capable of crossing the lipid neuronal membrane.

Local anesthetics are weak bases (pKa typically between 7.6 and 9.0). According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation (pH = pKa + log [Base]/[Cation]), only the uncharged (non-ionized) free base form can permeate through the hydrophobic lipid bilayer of the neuronal membrane. Once inside the axoplasm, the drug equilibrates and the protonated (ionized) cation binds to the inner pore of the voltage-gated Na+ channel. In inflamed or infected tissues, the extracellular pH drops substantially (to pH 5.5-6.0). In this acidic environment, the drug is overwhelmingly protonated (ionized), leaving virtually no lipophilic uncharged drug available to cross the axonal membrane, resulting in profound anesthetic failure.

• Option A is incorrect: Bacteria do not degrade lidocaine via specific amidases.
• Option C is incorrect: Acidosis does not denature the sodium channel.
• Option D is incorrect: Lidocaine does not precipitate at acidic pH; it is actually more water-soluble when protonated.
• Option E is incorrect: Nodes of Ranvier do not close mechanically.

stem: A 45-year-old man undergoes an ultrasound-guided femoral nerve block using 0.5% bupivacaine. Ten minutes later, he complains of perioral numbness, metallic taste, and dizziness, rapidly followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures, wide-complex ventricular tachycardia, and severe cardiovascular collapse (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity, LAST). In addition to airway control and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, which of the following is the specific antidote of choice to reverse local anesthetic cardiotoxicity?

options.text: Intravenous 20% lipid emulsion ('lipid rescue')
Intravenous calcium gluconate
Intravenous flumazenil
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous naloxone

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Intravenous 20% lipid emulsion ('lipid rescue').

Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) is a life-threatening complication resulting from accidental intravascular injection or rapid systemic absorption of high doses of local anesthetics (particularly highly lipophilic agents like bupivacaine). Bupivacaine strongly blocks cardiac voltage-gated Na+ channels and inhibits myocardial fatty acid oxidation. The definitive treatment for LAST is intravenous 20% lipid emulsion (e.g., Intralipid). Lipid emulsion acts as a 'lipid sink' (extracting the lipophilic anesthetic from myocardial and brain tissue into an intravascular lipid partition) and directly overcomes metabolic inhibition, rapidly restoring cardiac conduction and contractility.

• Option B is incorrect: Calcium gluconate stabilizes cardiac membranes in hyperkalemia, but is ineffective in LAST.
• Option C is incorrect: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; it does not reverse local anesthetics and may trigger seizures.
• Option D is incorrect: Sodium bicarbonate treats TCA toxicity and metabolic acidosis, but is not the primary rescue agent for LAST.
• Option E is incorrect: Naloxone reverses opioid overdose.

stem: A neuropharmacologist is contrasting the molecular mechanisms of phenobarbital (a barbiturate) versus lorazepam (a benzodiazepine) on the GABA-A receptor. Why are barbiturates associated with a significantly higher risk of fatal respiratory depression and toxicity in overdose compared to benzodiazepines?

options.text: Barbiturates increase the frequency of chloride channel opening, whereas benzodiazepines increase channel duration
Barbiturates increase the duration of chloride channel opening and can directly open chloride channels at high concentrations even in the complete absence of GABA
Barbiturates irreversibly block astrocytic GABA reuptake transporters
Barbiturates act as full agonists at NMDA glutamate receptors
Barbiturates lack hepatic metabolism and accumulate indefinitely in adipose tissue

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Barbiturates increase the duration of chloride channel opening and can directly open chloride channels at high concentrations even in the complete absence of GABA.

Barbiturates and benzodiazepines both enhance GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission, but through fundamentally distinct allosteric actions: (1) Benzodiazepines increase the FREQUENCY of channel opening in response to GABA, but cannot open the channel independently of endogenous GABA. (2) Barbiturates prolong the DURATION of chloride channel opening ('barbiDURATe'). Crucially, at high concentrations, barbiturates become GABA-mimetic, directly opening the chloride pore even without GABA present. This ability to directly activate chloride conductance produces profound, unchecked CNS and medullary respiratory depression, leading to a much lower therapeutic index and high overdose fatality.

• Option A is incorrect: It reverses the mechanisms (BZD = frequency, Barbiturate = duration).
• Option C is incorrect: Tiagabine blocks GABA reuptake (GAT-1), not barbiturates.
• Option D is incorrect: Barbiturates actually inhibit AMPA receptors, they do not stimulate NMDA receptors.
• Option E is incorrect: Barbiturates are metabolized by hepatic P450 enzymes (and are potent CYP inducers).

stem: On an axial non-contrast brain CT scan of an 82-year-old patient, dense, symmetric bilateral calcifications are visualized in the posterior aspect of the lateral ventricles at the junction where the body, occipital horn, and temporal horn meet (the atrium / trigone). What normal anatomical structure is this, and what is its clinical significance?

options.text: Calcified glomus of the choroid plexus; a common normal physiological finding that should not be mistaken for an intraventricular hemorrhage
Bilateral colloid cysts of the third ventricle
Ependymoma of the fourth ventricle
Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
Calcification of the caudate nucleus head

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Calcified glomus of the choroid plexus; a common normal physiological finding that should not be mistaken for an intraventricular hemorrhage.

The atrium (trigone) of the lateral ventricle is the confluence of the ventricular body, occipital (posterior) horn, and temporal (inferior) horn. Within the atrium, the choroid plexus forms a prominent enlargement called the Glomus of the choroid plexus. Physiological calcification of the glomus is extremely common with advancing age (seen in >50% of elderly adults) and appears as dense, symmetrical hyperdensities on CT. Recognizing this normal anatomical variant prevents misinterpretation as intraventricular hemorrhage or intraventricular neoplasm.

• Option B is incorrect: Colloid cysts occur at the roof of the 3rd ventricle near the foramen of Monro, not in the lateral ventricular trigone.
• Option C is incorrect: Ependymomas typically arise from the floor of the 4th ventricle in children.
• Option D is incorrect: SEGAs arise near the foramen of Monro in tuberous sclerosis.
• Option E is incorrect: The head of the caudate bulges into the lateral wall of the anterior (frontal) horn.

stem: The electrogenic Na+/K+-ATPase pump is vital for maintaining resting neuronal membrane potential and cellular volume. Which of the following statements correctly describes the stoichiometry and direct electrophysiological effect of this pump?

options.text: It exports 2 Na+ ions and imports 3 K+ ions per ATP, producing a net positive inward current

It exports 3 Na+ ions out of the cell and imports 2 K+ ions into the cell per ATP molecule hydrolyzed, generating a net outward current that contributes directly (-3 to -5 mV) to membrane hyperpolarization
It transports equal numbers of Na+ and K+ ions, having no net effect on membrane charge
It moves Na+ down its concentration gradient to pump Ca2+ out of the cell
It is localized exclusively to the postsynaptic dendritic spine density

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. It exports 3 Na+ ions out of the cell and imports 2 K+ ions into the cell per ATP molecule hydrolyzed, generating a net outward current that contributes directly (-3 to -5 mV) to membrane hyperpolarization.

The Na+/K+-ATPase is an electrogenic P-type ATPase that consumes roughly 50-70% of total neuronal ATP. With each ATP hydrolyzed, it pumps 3 Na+ ions OUT of the intracellular space and 2 K+ ions IN. Because 3 positive charges leave while only 2 positive charges enter, the pump creates a net outward positive current (net loss of 1 positive charge per cycle), making the inside of the membrane slightly more negative (-3 to -5 mV hyperpolarizing contribution). Its principal role is maintaining the low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+ gradients necessary for action potentials and secondary active transport.

• Option A is incorrect: It reverses the stoichiometry (it is 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, not vice versa).
• Option C is incorrect: The pump is electrogenic, not electrically neutral.
• Option D is incorrect: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) moves Na+ down its gradient to export Ca2+; it does not consume ATP directly.
• Option E is incorrect: The Na+/K+ pump is distributed throughout the entire neuronal axolemma, soma, and glia, especially clustered at nodes of Ranvier.

stem: A neurobiology researcher uses a cell-permeable peptide that selectively inhibits the GTPase activity of dynamin in cultured cortical neurons. Following high-frequency electrical stimulation of the neurons, which of the following processes will be blocked at the presynaptic nerve terminal?

options.text: Vesicular exocytosis triggered by synaptotagmin
Pinching off (scission) of clathrin-coated endocytic vesicles from the presynaptic plasma membrane during synaptic vesicle recycling
Docking of vesicles via syntaxin and synaptobrevin
Proton pumping by vesicular V-ATPase
Axonal transport of mitochondria along microtubules

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Pinching off (scission) of clathrin-coated endocytic vesicles from the presynaptic plasma membrane during synaptic vesicle recycling.

Following neurotransmitter exocytosis, the presynaptic terminal must rapidly recycle vesicular membrane components to sustain high-frequency transmission. Vesicular proteins are retrieved via clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Clathrin coats assemble around invaginating membranes, forming coated pits. Dynamin, a large mechanochemical GTPase, forms a polymeric collar around the neck of the invaginating vesicle and hydrolyzes GTP to pinch off ('scission') the vesicle from the plasma membrane. Inhibiting dynamin leads to a massive accumulation of unpinched, invaginated coated pits at the axolemma and rapid depletion of the readily releasable vesicle pool.

• Option A is incorrect: Synaptotagmin Ca2+ sensing and exocytosis occur before endocytic retrieval.
• Option C is incorrect: SNARE-mediated docking precedes membrane fusion.
• Option D is incorrect: The vacuolar H+-ATPase acidifies the recycled vesicle to provide the electrochemical proton gradient driving neurotransmitter loading.
• Option E is incorrect: Microtubular transport is driven by kinesin (anterograde) and dynein (retrograde), not dynamin.

stem: A 19-year-old college student presents to the emergency department with severe agitation, hyperthermia (104.2°F / 40.1°C), hypertension (190/110 mm Hg), tachycardia (140 bpm), dilated pupils (mydriasis), diaphoresis, and paranoia after consuming a party drug. Laboratory testing confirms acute amphetamine intoxication. What is the cellular mechanism by which amphetamines cause massive release of monoamines (dopamine and norepinephrine) into the synaptic cleft?

options.text: Direct agonism at postsynaptic adrenergic and dopamine receptors
Substrate displacement of monoamines from vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) into the cytoplasm, followed by reverse transport of monoamines through DAT and NET into the synaptic cleft
Irreversible suicide inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT)
Blocking potassium channels to cause prolonged presynaptic calcium influx
Stimulating acetylcholine synthesis in postganglionic sympathetic terminals

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Substrate displacement of monoamines from vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) into the cytoplasm, followed by reverse transport of monoamines through DAT and NET into the synaptic cleft.

Amphetamines exert a potent, multi-pronged sympathomimetic effect through non-vesicular release: (1) They enter presynaptic terminals via dopamine (DAT) and norepinephrine (NET) transporters, (2) They inhibit and disrupt the pH gradient of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), causing displacement and leakage of stored dopamine and norepinephrine from synaptic vesicles into the axoplasm, (3) They inhibit monoamine oxidase (MAO), preventing intraneuronal breakdown, and (4) They reverse the transport direction of DAT and NET (via phosphorylation), pumping free cytosolic monoamines backwards OUT of the terminal into the synaptic cleft independently of action potentials. In contrast, cocaine simply blocks DAT/NET/SERT reuptake.

• Option A is incorrect: Amphetamine does not act as a direct receptor agonist.
• Option C is incorrect: Entacapone and tolcapone inhibit COMT, not amphetamine.
• Option D is incorrect: Amphetamine release is non-exocytic and Ca2+-independent.
• Option E is incorrect: Sympathetic postganglionic terminals release norepinephrine, not acetylcholine (except sweat glands).

stem: During repetitive, high-frequency neuronal firing in the hippocampus, local extracellular potassium concentration rises from 3 mM to over 10 mM, which would depolarize neighboring neurons and trigger unconstrained seizure activity if left uncorrected. Astrocytes rapidly clear this excess extracellular K+ and disperse it across an interconnected astrocytic syncytium. What specialized channels and intercellular junctions mediate this astrocytic 'spatial potassium buffering'?

options.text: Inward-rectifying potassium (Kir4.1) channels on astrocyte membranes and gap junctions (connexin 43) connecting astrocytes
Voltage-gated sodium channels and desmosomes
Ligand-gated chloride channels and tight junctions (claudin 5)
L-type calcium channels and hemidesmosomes
Aquaporin-1 channels and focal adhesions

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Inward-rectifying potassium (Kir4.1) channels on astrocyte membranes and gap junctions (connexin 43) connecting astrocytes.

During intense neuronal activity, K+ efflux into the narrow extracellular space threatens to depolarize resting membrane potentials. Astrocytes perform 'spatial potassium buffering': (1) Astrocytes express high levels of inwardly rectifying potassium channels (Kir4.1), which take up excess K+ from regions of high extracellular concentration; (2) Astrocytes are extensively coupled to one another via gap junctions composed of Connexin 43, forming a vast functional syncytium; (3) The accumulated K+ is rapidly redistributed through the syncytium and extruded into distant regions with lower K+ concentrations (e.g., around cerebral blood vessels). Loss-of-function mutations in Kir4.1 cause EAST syndrome (epilepsy, ataxia, sensorineural deafness, and tubulopathy).

• Option B is incorrect: Astrocytes do not fire sodium action potentials or use desmosomes for buffering.
• Option C is incorrect: Claudin-5 forms tight junctions between endothelial cells of the BBB.
• Option D is incorrect: L-type calcium channels do not clear potassium.
• Option E is incorrect: Aquaporin-4 (not AQP1) is localized to astrocytic end-feet for water homeostasis and glymphatics.

stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes resection of a brain tumor. Histopathological examination of the surrounding non-neoplastic brain tissue reveals extensive astrogliosis (reactive gliosis) characterized by hypertrophy of astrocytic cell bodies and thick, elongated cytoplasmic processes packed with intermediate filaments. Immunohistochemical staining confirms robust upregulation of which intermediate filament protein, which serves as a definitive biomarker for astrocytes?

options.text: Desmin
Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP)
Vimentin exclusively
Cytokeratin
Neurofilament light chain

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP).

In response to any central nervous system injury (ischemia, trauma, infection, neurodegeneration, or surgical margins), astrocytes undergo reactive astrogliosis. This process involves cellular hypertrophy, proliferation, and dramatic upregulation of Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP), a class III intermediate filament unique to mature astrocytes and ependymal cells. Reactive astrocytes extend dense overlapping processes to wall off the injury site and form a permanent physical and chemical barrier known as the 'glial scar'. GFAP is also a diagnostic immunohistochemical marker for astrocytic tumors (e.g., pilocytic astrocytoma, glioblastoma).

• Option A is incorrect: Desmin is an intermediate filament marker for muscle cells.
• Option C is incorrect: Vimentin is present in mesenchymal cells and immature glia, but GFAP is the specific marker for mature astrocytes.
• Option D is incorrect: Cytokeratins are intermediate filaments of epithelial cells.
• Option E is incorrect: Neurofilaments are the intermediate filaments of neurons.

stem: A 65-year-old man with Parkinson disease is prescribed oral levodopa (L-DOPA) combined with carbidopa. Plain dopamine cannot be administered systemically because it fails to cross the blood-brain barrier. How does L-DOPA successfully cross the capillary endothelial cells of the blood-brain barrier into the cerebral parenchyma?

options.text: Passive non-ionic diffusion through endothelial lipid membranes
Carrier-mediated transport via the Large Neutral Amino Acid Transporter 1 (LAT1)
Receptor-mediated endocytosis via the transferrin receptor
Active retrograde pinocytosis through pericytes
Convective bulk flow through endothelial fenestrations

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Carrier-mediated transport via the Large Neutral Amino Acid Transporter 1 (LAT1).

The blood-brain barrier lacks fenestrations and has tight junctions, preventing polar monoamines like dopamine (which has a positive charge at physiological pH and lacks lipid solubility) from entering the brain. Levodopa (L-DOPA), the immediate amino acid precursor of dopamine, is recognized as a substrate by the Large Neutral Amino Acid Transporter 1 (LAT1, SLC7A5) expressed on both luminal and abluminal membranes of brain capillary endothelial cells. LAT1 transports L-DOPA into the brain via facilitated diffusion, where central DOPA decarboxylase converts it into dopamine. High-protein meals compete for LAT1 and can decrease L-DOPA absorption ('on-off' phenomenon).

• Option A is incorrect: L-DOPA is polar and cannot cross by passive simple diffusion.
• Option C is incorrect: Transferrin receptor mediates iron uptake, not L-DOPA.
• Option D is incorrect: Pericytes do not transport L-DOPA by retrograde pinocytosis.
• Option E is incorrect: Cerebral capillary endothelial cells lack fenestrations.

stem: A radiologist is reviewing an axial T2-weighted MRI of the brain and pointing out the anatomical boundaries of the lateral ventricles to a medical student. What structure forms the curved lateral wall of the anterior (frontal) horn of the lateral ventricle, bulging into the ventricular lumen?

options.text: Head of the caudate nucleus
Globus pallidus
Hippocampus
Putamen
Anterior commissure

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Head of the caudate nucleus.

The anterior (frontal) horn of the lateral ventricle is bounded by: (1) Medially: the vertical septum pellucidum; (2) Superiorly and anteriorly (roof and anterior wall): the genu and body of the corpus callosum; (3) Laterally: the prominent rounded head of the caudate nucleus. In Huntington disease, bilateral atrophy of the caudate head removes this normal lateral convexity, resulting in characteristic box-car / squared-off enlargement of the frontal horns on MRI/CT.

• Option B is incorrect: Globus pallidus lies lateral to the internal capsule, deep within the hemispheric white matter.
• Option C is incorrect: The hippocampus bulges into the floor and medial wall of the INFERIOR (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle.
• Option D is incorrect: The putamen lies lateral to the internal capsule and globus pallidus.
• Option E is incorrect: The anterior commissure lies at the rostral boundary of the 3rd ventricle.

stem: During a neurosurgery case involving endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), the surgeon navigates an endoscope into the third ventricle. On the floor of the third ventricle, which of the following midline neuroendocrine structures serves as an essential anatomical landmark situated immediately posterior to the optic chiasm and optic recess?

options.text: Infundibulum (pituitary stalk) and tuber cinereum
Pineal gland
Colloid cyst cavity
Posterior commissure
Facial colliculus

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Infundibulum (pituitary stalk) and tuber cinereum.

The third ventricle is a narrow, slit-like cavity situated in the midline of the diencephalon between the two thalami. Its floor, moving anterior to posterior, consists of: the optic chiasm, the infundibular recess (giving rise to the pituitary stalk/infundibulum), the tuber cinereum, the paired mammillary bodies, and the posterior perforated substance extending to the midbrain tegmentum. During endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV), the surgeon perforates the thin, translucent floor of the third ventricle between the infundibular recess and the mammillary bodies into the prepontine/interpeduncular cistern to bypass aqueductal stenosis.

• Option B is incorrect: The pineal gland is attached to the posterior wall/epithalamus of the 3rd ventricle above the posterior commissure.
• Option C is incorrect: Colloid cysts are pathological cysts located at the roof near the foramen of Monro.
• Option D is incorrect: Posterior commissure lies on the posterior wall.
• Option E is incorrect: Facial colliculus is located in the rhomboid fossa of the 4th ventricle.

stem: On the floor of the fourth ventricle (rhomboid fossa), a distinct round prominence known as the facial colliculus is visible in the medial pontine tegmentum. Which underlying cranial nerve motor nucleus and axonal loop form this bulge?

options.text: Facial nerve (CN VII) motor nucleus looped by abducens nerve (CN VI) fibers
Abducens nerve (CN VI) motor nucleus looped internally by motor fibers of the facial nerve (CN VII)
Trochlear nerve (CN IV) nucleus looped by oculomotor nerve (CN III) fibers
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) nucleus looped by the solitary tract
Trigeminal motor nucleus looped by sensory fibers of the spinal trigeminal tract

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Abducens nerve (CN VI) motor nucleus looped internally by motor fibers of the facial nerve (CN VII).

The facial colliculus is a prominent landmark on the dorsal surface of the pons in the floor of the fourth ventricle. It is formed by the underlying abducens (CN VI) nucleus, which is encircled dorsally by axons of the facial motor (CN VII) nucleus (the internal genu of the facial nerve) before they exit anterolaterally. A lesion at the facial colliculus (e.g., pontine glioma, infarction, or MS plaque) produces a combined ipsilateral lateral gaze paralysis (CN VI palsy) and complete ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis (CN VII Bell's-type palsy).

• Option A is incorrect: It reverses the nucleus and the looping fibers.
• Option C is incorrect: CN IV exits the dorsal midbrain beneath the inferior colliculi.
• Option D is incorrect: The hypoglossal trigone lies inferiorly in the medullary portion of the rhomboid fossa.
• Option E is incorrect: Trigeminal motor nucleus is located in the mid-pons and does not form a collicular bulge in the 4th ventricle.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a Chiari I malformation presents with progressive weakness and muscle wasting in both hands, accompanied by painless burns on her fingers from cooking. Neurological examination reveals bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation across her upper chest, neck, and arms, with preserved light touch, vibration, and joint position sense. In her hands, there is marked intrinsic muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and bilateral absent triceps and biceps reflexes. How does the pathological expansion of a cervical syringomyelia produce both sensory dissociation and lower motor neuron weakness in the hands?

options.text: The cavity initially compresses the posterior columns, then extends laterally into the sympathetic chain
The syrinx initially destroys decussating second-order spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, and subsequent lateral extension destroys anterior horn alpha motor neurons
The syrinx causes selective demyelination of dorsal root ganglia, sparing ventral roots
The fluid pressure blocks cerebrospinal fluid flow through the posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The syrinx damages descending corticospinal fibers without affecting spinal gray matter

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. The syrinx initially destroys decussating second-order spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, and subsequent lateral extension destroys anterior horn alpha motor neurons.

Syringomyelia begins as a cystic longitudinal cavity (syrinx) centered near the central canal of the spinal cord (most frequently C2-T1). (1) Sensory dissociation: The expanding syrinx first compresses and transects the second-order nociceptive axons of the anterolateral system (ALS) as they decussate across the anterior white commissure. This produces a bilateral, 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature over the corresponding dermatomes, while light touch and dorsal column vibration/proprioception remain spared. (2) LMN weakness: As the syrinx enlarges radially and laterally, it directly invades and destroys the ventral (anterior) gray horns, destroying alpha motor neurons and producing lower motor neuron signs (flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and areflexia) in the upper extremities.

• Option A is incorrect: Posterior columns lie dorsal to the central canal and are spared until late; the syrinx does not reach the paravertebral sympathetic chain.
• Option C is incorrect: DRGs are outside the spinal cord in the intervertebral foramina.
• Option D is incorrect: Syrinx is within the spinal cord parenchyma, not compressing cerebellar arteries.
• Option E is incorrect: Damage to anterior horn cells (gray matter) produces LMN signs; damage to corticospinal tracts (white matter) would produce spastic paraparesis below the lesion (UMN signs).

stem: A 44-year-old man recovers from a severe episode of pneumococcal meningitis. Four months later, he presents with progressive headaches, lethargy, cognitive slowing, and bilateral papilledema. Brain MRI reveals marked, symmetrical dilation of all four cerebral ventricles (lateral, third, and fourth ventricles) without any intraventricular mass or focal structural obstruction. What is the pathological mechanism responsible for this communicating hydrocephalus?

options.text: Aqueductal stenosis secondary to ependymal scarring
Fibrosis and obliteration of the arachnoid granulations (villi) by purulent meningeal exudate, preventing CSF resorption into the dural venous sinuses
Choroid plexus papilloma causing massive CSF hypersecretion
Herniation of the cerebellar tonsils obstructing the foramen magnum
Atresia of the foramina of Luschka and Magendie

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Fibrosis and obliteration of the arachnoid granulations (villi) by purulent meningeal exudate, preventing CSF resorption into the dural venous sinuses.

Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF flow through the ventricular channels is completely unobstructed, but its absorption into the venous system is impaired. Following bacterial meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage, inflammatory exudate, debris, and red blood cells enter the subarachnoid space and arachnoid granulations (villi). Subsequent chronic organizing fibrosis (obliterative arachnoiditis) clogs the microscopic arachnoid villi, preventing CSF resorption into the superior sagittal sinus. Because CSF continues to be produced at ~500 mL/day, fluid accumulates upstream, symmetrically dilating all four ventricles (lateral, 3rd, and 4th) under elevated intracranial pressure.

• Option A is incorrect: Aqueductal stenosis spares the 4th ventricle (non-communicating hydrocephalus).
• Option C is incorrect: Choroid plexus papilloma is a rare childhood tumor; post-meningitis hydrocephalus is absorptive failure, not hypersecretion.
• Option D is incorrect: Tonsillar herniation is a consequence of increased ICP, not the primary cause of hydrocephalus.
• Option E is incorrect: Atresia of foramina of Luschka/Magendie is congenital Dandy-Walker malformation.

stem: In the neurointensive care management of patients with severe traumatic brain injury and elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) must be rigorously maintained to prevent secondary ischemic injury. How is cerebral perfusion pressure calculated, and what is the minimum recommended CPP target in adults?

options.text: CPP = Systolic BP - ICP; Target > 120 mm Hg
CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - Intracranial Pressure (ICP); Target 60 to 70 mm Hg
CPP = Diastolic BP + Central Venous Pressure; Target 30 to 40 mm Hg
CPP = MAP / ICP; Target > 4.0
CPP = Pulse Pressure * Respiratory Rate; Target 80 to 90 mm Hg

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - Intracranial Pressure (ICP); Target 60 to 70 mm Hg.

Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) represents the net pressure gradient driving blood flow and oxygen delivery to the cerebral capillary bed. It is defined mathematically as: CPP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - Intracranial Pressure (ICP) [where MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP)]. In healthy individuals, autoregulation maintains constant cerebral blood flow across a CPP range of 50–150 mm Hg. In neurotrauma or elevated ICP, CPP < 60 mm Hg leads to critical cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemia, and worsening cytotoxic edema, whereas CPP > 70 mm Hg can induce hyperperfusion and ARDS. Neurocritical care guidelines target CPP between 60 and 70 mm Hg.

• Options A, C, D, and E represent incorrect formulas and physiological targets.

stem: A 26-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent and her husband are planning their first pregnancy and consult a medical geneticist for preconception carrier screening. The genetic counselor orders a targeted screening panel for several autosomal recessive sphingolipidoses common in this population. For which of the following combinations of disorders should carrier status be assessed?

options.text: Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher disease, and Niemann-Pick disease
Huntington disease, Fragile X syndrome, and Marfan syndrome
Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Hemophilia A, and Fabry disease
Neurofibromatosis type 1, Tuberous sclerosis, and Von Hippel-Lindau disease
Myotonic dystrophy, Friedrich ataxia, and Spinocerebellar ataxia

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher disease, and Niemann-Pick disease.

Due to founder effects and historical population bottlenecks, individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry have a significantly increased carrier frequency for several severe autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders: (1) Tay-Sachs disease (carrier rate ~1 in 27-30; hexosaminidase A deficiency), (2) Gaucher disease (carrier rate ~1 in 15-18; glucocerebrosidase deficiency), (3) Niemann-Pick disease type A (carrier rate ~1 in 90; sphingomyelinase deficiency), along with Bloom syndrome, Canavan disease, and Fanconi anemia. Preconception carrier screening is standard of care to identify at-risk couples.

• Option B is incorrect: Huntington and Marfan are autosomal dominant; Fragile X is X-linked triplet repeat.
• Option C is incorrect: DMD, Hemophilia A, and Fabry are X-linked recessive disorders.
• Option D is incorrect: NF1, TSC, and VHL are autosomal dominant tumor suppressor syndromes.
• Option E is incorrect: These are trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders.

stem: A biochemist is analyzing maternal blood samples to evaluate the biochemical pathway linking folate metabolism to neural tube defect prevention. In the folate cycle, 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate is reduced by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF). Which subsequent reaction transfers the methyl group from 5-MTHF to homocysteine to generate methionine, requiring Vitamin B12 as a mandatory cofactor?

options.text: Methionine synthase
Cystathionine beta-synthase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Thymidylate synthase
Serine hydroxymethyltransferase

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Methionine synthase.

Folate and vitamin B12 metabolism are tightly intertwined through Methionine Synthase: 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) transfers its methyl group to vitamin B12 (cobalamin), forming methylcobalamin, which then transfers the methyl group to homocysteine to synthesize methionine. Methionine is then activated to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor required for DNA methylation and epigenetic regulation during embryogenesis. Concurrently, tetrahydrofolate (THF) is regenerated to enter purine and thymidylate synthesis for rapid neural progenitor mitosis. In vitamin B12 deficiency, folate is trapped as 5-MTHF ('folate trap'), causing secondary functional folate deficiency and homocysteine accumulation.

• Option B is incorrect: Cystathionine β-synthase converts homocysteine to cystathionine and requires Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine).
• Option C is incorrect: Dihydrofolate reductase converts DHF to THF using NADPH (inhibited by methotrexate).
• Option D is incorrect: Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP using 5,10-methylene-THF (inhibited by 5-fluorouracil).
• Option E is incorrect: SHMT reversibly interconverts glycine and serine.

stem: A pediatrician examines a healthy 4-month-old infant. The Moro reflex (startle response to sudden head extension) and rooting reflex are easily elicited. By what age should these primitive infant reflexes disappear under normal neurodevelopmental conditions, and what neurological process accounts for their suppression?

options.text: By 4 to 6 months of age, due to descending inhibition from maturing frontal cerebral cortical circuits and myelination of the corticospinal tracts
By 2 weeks of age, due to apoptosis of brainstem motor neurons
By 3 years of age, due to closure of the cranial sutures
They normally persist throughout adult life as baseline defensive reflexes
By 12 months of age, due to loss of spinal motor neurons

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. By 4 to 6 months of age, due to descending inhibition from maturing frontal cerebral cortical circuits and myelination of the corticospinal tracts.

Primitive reflexes (e.g., Moro, rooting, palmar grasp, sucking) are primitive brainstem and spinal cord motor patterns present at birth. As postnatal CNS maturation proceeds, rapid myelination of descending corticospinal tracts and development of frontal cortical inhibitory networks exert supraspinal control, suppressing these reflexes by roughly 4 to 6 months of age (the Babinski reflex may persist up to 12-24 months until walking is established). Re-emergence of primitive reflexes in an adult ('frontal release signs': grasp, snout, palmomental reflexes) signifies bilateral frontal lobe pathology or advanced neurodegeneration (e.g., frontotemporal dementia, Alzheimer disease).

• Option B is incorrect: 2 weeks is far too early; primitive reflexes are robust throughout the first months.
• Option C is incorrect: Fontanelles close at 12-18 months, but primitive reflexes disappear much earlier.
• Option D is incorrect: Primitive reflexes disappear in normal adults; persistence or re-emergence is pathological.
• Option E is incorrect: Spinal motor neurons do not degenerate in normal maturation.

stem: A 3-year-old child with communicating hydrocephalus underwent placement of a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt 6 months ago. He is brought to the clinic because of severe, postural headaches that occur whenever he stands up or sits upright, and resolve completely within minutes of lying flat. His parents also note he has become irritable and vomits after prolonged upright activity. Brain MRI reveals bilateral slit-like collapsed lateral ventricles and small bilateral subdural fluid collections (subdural hygromas). What is the mechanism of his symptoms?

options.text: Complete shunt occlusion leading to acute intraventricular hypertension
Shunt overdrainage causing intracranial hypotension, downward brain sag, and stretching of pain-sensitive meninges and bridging veins
Bacterial colonization of the shunt with Propionibacterium acnes causing chronic ventriculitis
Peritoneal pseudocyst formation preventing abdominal CSF reabsorption
Malposition of the ventricular catheter into the third ventricle

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Shunt overdrainage causing intracranial hypotension, downward brain sag, and stretching of pain-sensitive meninges and bridging veins.

Shunt overdrainage is a recognized complication of VP shunts when the valve siphon pressure is set too low. Excessive siphoning of CSF in the upright posture drops intracranial pressure below atmospheric pressure (intracranial hypotension / slit-ventricle syndrome). This loss of buoyant CSF support causes the brain to sag downward, exerting painful traction on pain-sensitive dural structures (producing classic orthostatic / postural headaches: worse upright, relieved supine). Furthermore, as the cerebral hemispheres collapse away from the calvarium, traction on delicate bridging veins can produce tearing, subdural hygromas, or chronic subdural hematomas. Management involves upgrading to a programmable anti-siphon valve.

• Option A is incorrect: Shunt occlusion causes increased ICP with ventricular DILATION, headaches worse lying flat, and papilledema.
• Option C is incorrect: Infection causes fever, meningismus, shunt erythema, and inflammatory CSF.
• Option D is incorrect: Peritoneal pseudocyst impairs drainage, causing elevated ICP and shunt failure.
• Option E is incorrect: Catheter malposition does not selectively cause postural orthostatic headaches and collapsed slit ventricles.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fluctuating double vision and drooping of both eyelids that becomes progressively worse toward the evening, especially after long hours reading or working at her computer. Physical examination reveals bilateral ptosis that worsens after 60 seconds of sustained upward gaze. Applying an ice pack over her closed eyelids for 2 minutes produces significant resolution of the ptosis (positive ice pack test). Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz demonstrates a progressive decrement in compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude. What is the primary molecular target of the autoantibodies causing this condition?

options.text: Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the motor end plate
Synaptic acetylcholinesterase enzyme molecules
Presynaptic vesicle-associated membrane protein (synaptobrevin)
Ryanodine receptor type 1 on the sarcoplasmic reticulum

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the motor end plate.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder caused by autoantibodies directed against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the postsynaptic motor end plate (found in ~85% of generalized cases; the remainder frequently target muscle-specific kinase, MuSK). Binding of antibodies causes complement-mediated destruction and simplification of postsynaptic junctional folds, along with receptor cross-linking and internalization. This reduces the number of functional AChRs, lowering the amplitude of end plate potentials (EPP) below the threshold needed to trigger muscle action potentials. Fatigability occurs because physiological depletion of presynaptic ACh stores with repetitive use further drops EPP below threshold, producing the classic decremental response on slow (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation.

• Option A is incorrect: Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type VGCC cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS).
• Option C is incorrect: Acetylcholinesterase is inhibited by drugs like pyridostigmine or toxins like organophosphates, not targeted in MG.
• Option D is incorrect: Synaptobrevin is cleaved by botulinum neurotoxins B, D, F, G.
• Option E is incorrect: Ryanodine receptor mutations cause malignant hyperthermia.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with generalized myasthenia gravis after presenting with ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty chewing. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest is ordered as part of the initial diagnostic evaluation. What mediastinal pathology is most commonly associated with myasthenia gravis, for which surgical thymectomy offers a high probability of clinical improvement or complete remission?

options.text: Posterior mediastinal schwannoma
Thymic follicular hyperplasia (65-75%) or Thymoma (10-15%) in the anterior mediastinum
Middle mediastinal bronchogenic cyst
Substernal thyroid goiter extending into the tracheoesophageal groove
Small cell lung carcinoma with subcarinal lymphadenopathy

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Thymic follicular hyperplasia (65-75%) or Thymoma (10-15%) in the anterior mediastinum.

The thymus plays an essential role in the pathogenesis of myasthenia gravis. The normal thymus contains myoid cells that express nicotinic AChRs. In MG, the anterior mediastinum frequently harbors thymic abnormalities: approximately 65–75% of patients have thymic follicular hyperplasia (germinal center B-cell proliferation), and 10–15% have a thymoma (epithelial neoplasm of the thymus). Chest CT or MRI is mandatory in all newly diagnosed patients with MG. Surgical thymectomy removes the source of autoantigen sensitization and autoreactive T/B cells, leading to substantial clinical improvement or long-term medication-free remission.

• Option A is incorrect: Schwannomas are benign nerve sheath tumors located in the posterior mediastinum, not associated with MG.
• Option C is incorrect: Bronchogenic cysts are congenital anomalies of the middle mediastinum.
• Option D is incorrect: Substernal goiters arise from the thyroid gland; while autoimmune thyroiditis can co-occur with MG, thymic pathology is the primary driver.
• Option E is incorrect: Small cell lung cancer is associated with Lambert-Eaton syndrome, not MG.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive weakness in his thighs and hips. He has significant difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing stairs. He also reports dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction. On physical examination, his proximal lower extremity strength is initially 3/5, but after he performs maximum isometric knee extension for 10 seconds, his muscle strength temporarily increases to 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at rest but reappear immediately following brief exercise. High-frequency (20-50 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation shows a dramatic incremental increase (>100% CMAP facilitation). What is the underlying pathophysiology of this disorder?

options.text: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC)
Zinc metalloprotease cleavage of presynaptic SNAP-25
Degeneration of lower motor neurons in the spinal cord anterior horn
Toxin-mediated ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC).

Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder caused by autoantibodies directed against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) at the motor end plate and autonomic synapses. This blocks action-potential triggered calcium influx, preventing acetylcholine vesicle exocytosis and reducing baseline quantal release. Hallmark features include: (1) Proximal lower limb weakness (difficulty rising from chairs), (2) Autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, constipation) due to impaired parasympathetic/sympathetic transmission, (3) Hyporeflexia/areflexia, and (4) Post-exercise facilitation: brief muscle contraction or high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation accumulates residual intracellular calcium in the presynaptic terminal, overcoming the block and triggering an INCREMENTAL recruitment of CMAP (>100% increase). Over 50-60% of LEMS cases occur as a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).

• Option A is incorrect: MG features postsynaptic anti-AChR antibodies, decremental response, ocular weakness, and worsens with use.
• Option C is incorrect: Cleavage of SNAP-25 is the mechanism of botulinum toxin A and E.
• Option D is incorrect: Anterior horn cell loss characterizes Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).
• Option E is incorrect: Inactivation of EF-2 is the mechanism of Diphtheria and Pseudomonas exotoxins.

stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with severe constipation for 3 days, followed by poor feeding, a weak feeble cry, and inability to hold up her head. The parents report giving the infant small amounts of raw unpasteurized honey to soothe teething. On examination, the infant is lethargic, markedly hypotonic ('floppy baby'), with bilateral ptosis, sluggish pupillary light reflexes, and absent gag reflex. What is the cellular mechanism of the neurotoxin responsible for this infant's paralysis?

options.text: Blocks postsynaptic glycine receptors in spinal interneurons
Cleaves SNARE proteins (such as synaptobrevin and SNAP-25), preventing acetylcholine exocytosis at peripheral cholinergic synapses
Irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, leading to cholinergic exhaustion
Permanently opens voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing repolarization
Selectively destroys Schwann cells along motor cranial nerves

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Cleaves SNARE proteins (such as synaptobrevin and SNAP-25), preventing acetylcholine exocytosis at peripheral cholinergic synapses.

Infant botulism results from ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores (commonly found in raw honey or soil) that germinate in the immature infant gastrointestinal tract and produce botulinum neurotoxin in vivo. The toxin is a zinc metalloprotease consisting of a heavy chain (mediating endocytosis into cholinergic terminals) and a light chain. The light chain cleaves specific SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, synaptobrevin/VAMP, syntaxin) required for synaptic vesicle docking and fusion. This completely blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction (causing descending flaccid paralysis and hypotonia, 'floppy baby') and at parasympathetic autonomic ganglia/end organs (causing constipation, mydriasis, sluggish pupils, dry mouth). In contrast to foodborne botulism in adults (where preformed toxin is ingested), infant botulism involves active intraluminal bacterial colonization and toxin production; it is treated with human-derived botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG).

• Option A is incorrect: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) cleaves synaptobrevin in Renshaw cells and spinal inhibitory interneurons, blocking glycine and GABA release to cause spastic paralysis (trismus, risus sardonicus).
• Option C is incorrect: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition is the mechanism of organophosphates.
• Option D is incorrect: Opening voltage-gated Na+ channels is the mechanism of ciguatoxin and batrachotoxin.
• Option E is incorrect: Botulinum toxin does not damage Schwann cells.

stem: A 42-year-old farm worker is rushed to the emergency department after accidentally spraying himself with an undiluted organophosphate insecticide. He presents with diaphoresis, constricted pinpoint pupils (miosis), excessive salivation, lacrimation, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, wheezing with bilateral diffuse rales (bronchorrhea), and bradycardia. In addition, his extremities show diffuse muscle fasciculations and severe weakness. Which of the following two pharmacological agents must be administered immediately to reverse both his muscarinic and nicotinic toxic manifestations?

options.text: Physostigmine and Naloxone
Atropine (to block muscarinic receptors) and Pralidoxime (2-PAM, to regenerate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase at nicotinic and muscarinic synapses)
Scopolamine and Pyridostigmine
Epinephrine and Diphenhydramine
Flumazenil and Dantrolene

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Atropine (to block muscarinic receptors) and Pralidoxime (2-PAM, to regenerate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase at nicotinic and muscarinic synapses).

Organophosphates (e.g., malathion, parathion, sarin) are potent, irreversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE). They covalently phosphorylate the active-site serine residue of AChE, preventing acetylcholine hydrolysis and causing massive acetylcholine accumulation at: (1) Muscarinic receptors: leading to DUMBBELSS (Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchospasm/Bronchorrhea, Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation/Sweating); (2) Nicotinic receptors at the NMJ: leading to muscle fasciculations, cramping, and depolarizing flaccid muscle weakness/paralysis (including the diaphragm); and (3) CNS receptors: confusion, seizures, coma.

Management requires two complementary drugs: (1) Atropine: a competitive muscarinic receptor antagonist that rapidly crosses into the CNS, reverses bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and salivation (titrated until lung secretions clear; does NOT reverse muscle weakness/nicotinic effects); and (2) Pralidoxime (2-PAM): a nucleophilic oxime agent that binds to organophosphate-inhibited AChE and cleaves the phosphate-enzyme bond, regenerating active acetylcholinesterase at both nicotinic neuromuscular junctions (reversing skeletal muscle weakness and fasciculations) and muscarinic sites. Pralidoxime must be given early before chemical 'aging' (spontaneous dealkylation of the organophosphate-enzyme complex) permanently inactivates the enzyme.

• Option A is incorrect: Physostigmine is an AChE inhibitor and would worsen toxicity; naloxone treats opioids.
• Option C is incorrect: Pyridostigmine is an AChE inhibitor and would exacerbate organophosphate poisoning.
• Option D is incorrect: Epinephrine and diphenhydramine treat anaphylaxis, not cholinergic poisoning.
• Option E is incorrect: Flumazenil treats benzodiazepines; dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis maintained on oral pyridostigmine experiences a viral upper respiratory infection. Over 24 hours, she develops severe shortness of breath, inability to clear secretions, tachypnea, paradoxical abdominal breathing, and an inability to count past 10 in a single breath. Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF) is -15 cm H2O (normal < -60 cm H2O) and Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) is 12 mL/kg (critical < 15 mL/kg), indicating impending neuromuscular respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis). What is the most appropriate acute, life-saving disease-modifying treatment protocol?

options.text: Immediate escalation of pyridostigmine to quadruple the daily dose
Emergent intubation/ventilatory support combined with Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis) or Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg)
Immediate administration of high-dose succinylcholine to facilitate elective tracheostomy
Subcutaneous injection of edrophonium every 4 hours
Complete cessation of all medications without airway management

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Emergent intubation/ventilatory support combined with Plasma Exchange (Plasmapheresis) or Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg).

Myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening complication of myasthenia gravis defined by severe respiratory muscle weakness (diaphragm and intercostal muscles) and bulbar failure requiring mechanical ventilatory support. It is commonly precipitated by systemic infections, surgery, emotional stress, or medications (e.g., fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, beta-blockers, magnesium). Bedside pulmonary function tests (FVC < 15-20 mL/kg, NIF worse than -20 to -30 cm H2O) indicate the need for prompt elective endotracheal intubation. The acute disease-modifying treatments of choice are: (1) Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis, which physically removes pathogenic anti-AChR autoantibodies from the plasma) or (2) High-dose Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIg). High-dose corticosteroids are also initiated, but anticholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) are often temporarily paused or held while intubated to reduce airway secretions and avoid confusion with cholinergic crisis.

• Option A is incorrect: Escalating pyridostigmine during intubation causes excessive bronchial secretions and risks triggering a cholinergic crisis.
• Option C is incorrect: Succinylcholine is contraindicated; patients with MG are resistant to depolarizing blockers but prone to phase II block, and intubation is performed with careful airway management.
• Option D is incorrect: Edrophonium (Tensilon) is ultra-short acting (minutes) and used purely for diagnostic testing, not therapeutic maintenance.
• Option E is incorrect: Failing to manage the airway in impending respiratory arrest is fatal.

stem: An anesthesiologist is evaluating five different inhalational anesthetics for a surgical procedure. Anesthetic potency is defined by the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC). Which of the following statements correctly defines MAC, and how does MAC relate to the lipid:gas partition coefficient (oil:gas partition coefficient)?

options.text: MAC is the alveolar concentration that induces surgical anesthesia in 99% of patients; MAC is directly proportional to lipid solubility

MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration at 1 atmosphere that prevents movement in response to a standard surgical incision in 50% of patients; MAC is inversely proportional to lipid solubility (1/MAC = potency)
MAC represents the concentration of gas that dissolves in blood; high MAC indicates high blood solubility
MAC is the dose required to eliminate spontaneous breathing in 100% of patients; unrelated to lipid solubility
MAC is inversely proportional to the speed of induction; high MAC means fastest induction

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration at 1 atmosphere that prevents movement in response to a standard surgical incision in 50% of patients; MAC is inversely proportional to lipid solubility (1/MAC = potency).

Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) is the standardized measure of inhalational anesthetic potency. It is defined as the alveolar partial pressure (percentage of 1 atmosphere) of an inhaled anesthetic at steady state that prevents purposeful skeletal muscle movement in response to a standardized noxious surgical stimulus (skin incision) in 50% of subjects. According to the Meyer-Overton correlation, anesthetic potency is directly determined by lipid solubility: drugs with high lipid:gas (oil:gas) partition coefficients easily cross the hydrophobic neuronal lipid bilayer, requiring very low alveolar concentrations to achieve anesthesia (LOW MAC = HIGH POTENCY). Conversely, drugs with low lipid solubility (e.g., Nitrous Oxide, MAC = 104%) have very LOW potency and a HIGH MAC.

• Option A is incorrect: MAC represents the ED50 (50% of patients), not 99%; and MAC is inversely (not directly) related to lipid solubility.
• Option C is incorrect: Blood solubility is measured by the blood:gas partition coefficient, not MAC.
• Option D is incorrect: MAC measures somatic movement to pain in 50% of patients, not apnea.
• Option E is incorrect: Speed of induction is governed by the blood:gas partition coefficient, not MAC.

stem: During an operative case, an anesthesia resident needs an inhalational anesthetic that provides the most rapid rate of induction and the fastest, cleanest emergence (wake-up) from anesthesia, particularly in a morbidly obese patient. Which physical property of an inhaled gas determines the speed of anesthetic induction and emergence, and which commonly used volatile anesthetic possesses the lowest blood:gas partition coefficient?

options.text: Lipid:gas partition coefficient; Halothane
Blood:gas partition coefficient; Desflurane (0.42)
Molecular weight of the gas; Isoflurane
Vapor pressure at 20°C; Sevoflurane
Renal clearance rate; Enflurane

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Blood:gas partition coefficient; Desflurane (0.42).

The speed of induction and recovery (emergence) of an inhalational anesthetic is governed strictly by its solubility in blood, represented by the Blood:Gas Partition Coefficient:
1. Low blood:gas coefficient (insoluble in blood, e.g., Desflurane = 0.42, Nitrous Oxide = 0.47, Sevoflurane = 0.65): Very little gas dissolves in the blood reservoir. Consequently, the blood becomes saturated almost immediately, allowing alveolar partial pressure to rise rapidly and equilibrate quickly with brain partial pressure. This produces RAPID induction and RAPID emergence.
2. High blood:gas coefficient (highly soluble in blood, e.g., Halothane = 2.4, Isoflurane = 1.4): Blood acts as a large sponge that soaks up the gas. The alveolar and arterial partial pressures rise very slowly, delaying brain saturation and resulting in SLOW induction and SLOW emergence.
In morbidly obese patients, lipophilic gases also accumulate in adipose tissue; therefore, Desflurane's extremely low blood:gas coefficient (0.42) ensures the quickest emergence with minimal hangover.

• Option A is incorrect: Lipid:gas determines POTENCY (MAC), not speed of induction; halothane has very slow induction (blood:gas = 2.4).
• Option C is incorrect: Molecular weight does not determine induction speed.
• Option D is incorrect: Vapor pressure dictates vaporizer calibration, not induction velocity.
• Option E is incorrect: Inhalational agents are eliminated through alveolar exhalation, not renal clearance.

stem: A 22-year-old healthy man undergoes an emergency exploratory laparotomy following a blunt abdominal trauma. General anesthesia is induced with intravenous propofol, fentanyl, and succinylcholine, followed by endotracheal intubation. Anesthesia is maintained with inhaled sevoflurane.
